claim: Multicellular organisms have evolved from a unicellular ancestor at least 25 times.
source: Multicellular organisms have evolved from a unicellular ancestor at least 25 times (Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007), but we know little about what selected for the simplest form of multicellularity: an undifferentiated clump of cells produced by the repeated division of a single cell.
evidence: Supported by citation to Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007

claim: Protection from predation, environmental stress, and phagocytosis has been proposed as a driving force for multicellularity.
source: Two driving forces have been proposed, protection from a variety of factors (including predation [Kessin et al., 1996], environmental stress [Smukalla et al., 2008], and phagocytosis [Boraas et al., 1998]) and more efficient nutrient usage (Dworkin, 1972; Pfeiffer and Bonhoeffer, 2003; Koschwanez et al., 2011; Alegado et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kessin et al., 1996; Smukalla et al., 2008; and Boraas et al., 1998

claim: More efficient nutrient usage has been proposed as a driving force for multicellularity.
source: Two driving forces have been proposed, protection from a variety of factors (including predation [Kessin et al., 1996], environmental stress [Smukalla et al., 2008], and phagocytosis [Boraas et al., 1998]) and more efficient nutrient usage (Dworkin, 1972; Pfeiffer and Bonhoeffer, 2003; Koschwanez et al., 2011; Alegado et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dworkin, 1972; Pfeiffer and Bonhoeffer, 2003; Koschwanez et al., 2011; Alegado et al., 2012

claim: Sharing public goods favors clumps over isolated cells.
source: In earlier work, we showed that sharing public goods favors clumps over isolated cells and proposed that sharing could have selected for simple multicellularity (Koschwanez et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Koschwanez et al., 2011)

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae utilizes sucrose by secreting invertase.
source: The budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, utilizes sucrose by secreting invertase (Dodyk and Rothstein, 1964; Carlson et al., 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dodyk and Rothstein, 1964; Carlson et al., 1981

claim: Over 95% of invertase enzyme remains in the cell wall.
source: Over 95% of this enzyme remains in the cell wall (Esmon et al., 1987; Tammi et al., 1987), where it hydrolyzes sucrose into glucose and fructose, which are imported into the cell by a variety of hexose transporters (Meijer et al., 1996; Reifenberger et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Esmon et al., 1987; Tammi et al., 1987

claim: Invertase hydrolyzes sucrose into glucose and fructose in the cell wall.
source: Over 95% of this enzyme remains in the cell wall (Esmon et al., 1987; Tammi et al., 1987), where it hydrolyzes sucrose into glucose and fructose, which are imported into the cell by a variety of hexose transporters (Meijer et al., 1996; Reifenberger et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Esmon et al., 1987; Tammi et al., 1987; Meijer et al., 1996; Reifenberger et al., 1997

claim: Glucose and fructose are imported into the cell by a variety of hexose transporters.
source: Over 95% of this enzyme remains in the cell wall (Esmon et al., 1987; Tammi et al., 1987), where it hydrolyzes sucrose into glucose and fructose, which are imported into the cell by a variety of hexose transporters (Meijer et al., 1996; Reifenberger et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meijer et al., 1996; Reifenberger et al., 1997

claim: Lab yeast strains cannot grow from low density in low concentrations of sucrose because of diffusion.
source: Lab yeast strains cannot grow from low density in low concentrations of sucrose because of diffusion: each cell captures only a small fraction of the sugars that sucrose hydrolysis releases, and the molecules released by other, distant cells are at very low concentration.
evidence: Based on inference from the physical properties of diffusion and the spatial distribution of cells

claim: Forming multicellular clumps overcomes the failure to grow in low sucrose concentrations.
source: Forming multicellular clumps overcomes this failure; cells in a clump can capture glucose and fructose diffusing from their neighbors and grow in concentrations of sucrose where low concentrations of individual cells cannot.
evidence: Based on inference from the spatial arrangement of cells in clumps and diffusion properties

claim: Three engineered strategies allow yeast cells to grow on low sucrose: forming multicellular clumps, importing sucrose before hydrolyzing it, and increasing invertase expression.
source: We engineered and tested three strategies that allow yeast cells to grow on low sucrose: forming multicellular clumps, importing sucrose before hydrolyzing it, and increasing invertase expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2

claim: Of 12 successful clones, 11 formed multicellular clumps through incomplete cell separation.
source: Of 12 successful clones, 11 formed multicellular clumps through incomplete cell separation, 10 increased invertase expression, none imported sucrose, and 11 increased hexose transporter expression, a strategy we had not engineered.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from evolved populations

claim: Of 12 successful clones, 10 increased invertase expression.
source: Of 12 successful clones, 11 formed multicellular clumps through incomplete cell separation, 10 increased invertase expression, none imported sucrose, and 11 increased hexose transporter expression, a strategy we had not engineered.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from RNA sequencing

claim: None of the 12 successful clones imported sucrose.
source: Of 12 successful clones, 11 formed multicellular clumps through incomplete cell separation, 10 increased invertase expression, none imported sucrose, and 11 increased hexose transporter expression, a strategy we had not engineered.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from competition assays with suc2-1cyt strains

claim: Of 12 successful clones, 11 increased hexose transporter expression.
source: Of 12 successful clones, 11 formed multicellular clumps through incomplete cell separation, 10 increased invertase expression, none imported sucrose, and 11 increased hexose transporter expression, a strategy we had not engineered.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from RNA sequencing

claim: Increased hexose transporter expression was a strategy not anticipated by the researchers.
source: Of 12 successful clones, 11 formed multicellular clumps through incomplete cell separation, 10 increased invertase expression, none imported sucrose, and 11 increased hexose transporter expression, a strategy we had not engineered.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text

claim: Mal11 is a maltose importer that can also import sucrose.
source: Mal11 is a maltose importer that can also import sucrose (Stambuk et al., 1999), but is not expressed in our yeast strains (Brown et al., 2010).

claim: Mal11 is not expressed in the lab yeast strains used in this study.

claim: SUC2 and suc2-1cyt strains that make the maltose importer can grow from single cells on as little as 1 mM sucrose.
source: Figure 2B shows that both the SUC2 and suc2-1cyt strains that make the maltose importer can grow from single cells on as little as 1 mM sucrose.

claim: The importer makes extracellular sucrose digestion dispensable.
source: The nearly identical growth of the SUC2 and suc2-1cyt strains shows that the importer makes extracellular sucrose digestion dispensable, and the failure of the suc2Δ strains to grow shows that sucrose utilization after import still requires invertase.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data comparing SUC2 and suc2-1cyt strains

claim: Sucrose utilization after import still requires invertase.
source: The nearly identical growth of the SUC2 and suc2-1cyt strains shows that the importer makes extracellular sucrose digestion dispensable, and the failure of the suc2Δ strains to grow shows that sucrose utilization after import still requires invertase.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data showing suc2Δ strains fail to grow

claim: The three engineered strains all outcompeted the ancestral wild-type lab strain in 1 mM sucrose.

source: The three engineered strains all outcompeted the ancestral wild-type lab strain in 1 mM sucrose (Table 1), although the strain engineered to express increased invertase (EngHiInvertase) was a much worse competitor than the other two (EngClumpy, EngSucImport).

claim: Over 25–35 serial dilutions, the time it took the culture to become cloudy fell from 2 weeks to 3 days.

claim: All 10 populations displayed a clumpy phenotype.

This result confirms that the clumpiness in EvoClone2 is caused by the loss of function mutation in ACE2.
